title: The sales assistant that wanted every key
scenario:
You are a sales operations manager at a furniture wholesaler with 90 sales reps. The team wants its AI assistant to work with the company's systems, not only answer from its general knowledge.

An eager vendor sent a proposal. The sales director asks you to review it before Friday. The exhibit shows the proposal.
exhibit:
Integration proposal (made-up example data)

Goal: "Let the assistant do everything a sales rep can do."

#  System          What the assistant could do               Approval
1  CRM             search accounts, read deal notes          none
2  CRM             change deal values, close deals           none
3  Email           send emails to clients as the rep         none
4  Price list      read current prices                       none
5  Order system    look up order status                      none

Vendor note: "The model runs these actions directly inside your
systems, so no extra software is needed on your side."

Plan: build a separate custom link for each of your 2 AI apps
to each of the 4 systems.

questions.prompt: The vendor note says the model runs the actions directly inside your systems. What is the accurate picture?

options.text: Correct: modern models log in to business systems and click through them like a user.
options.explanation: Both vendors' docs describe a structured request that an application runs. The model doesn't operate the system itself.

options.text: Correct for your own tools: once you define a function, the model runs it inside your system.
options.explanation: Anthropic's page says client tools, which you define, run in your application. Your code runs them, not the model.

options.text: The model returns a structured tool call, and an application runs it and sends back the result.
options.explanation: Right. Anthropic's tool use page and OpenAI's function calling guide both describe this round trip. The application is where limits and checks live.

options.text: The model sends plain text, and a person on the vendor's team types it into each system.
options.explanation: The docs describe a structured call that software runs, not manual work by the vendor.

questions.prompt: Which rows carry the highest risk, and why?

options.text: Rows 2 and 3: they change records or send email, so a mistake has a real effect.
options.explanation: Right. The MCP spec's examples put taking actions (like writing data) under tools, apart from data for context. A wrong read shows bad data; a wrong write changes the world.

options.text: Rows 1 and 4: they read the most data, so they cost the most and are the riskiest.
options.explanation: Reading has risks too, but rows 2 and 3 can change deals or contact clients. Those effects are harder to undo.

options.text: Row 5 only: order data is the most sensitive data that a sales team ever handles.
options.explanation: Order status is a lookup. Changing deal values and emailing clients have bigger effects.

options.text: All five rows carry the same risk, because the same model is used for every one.
options.explanation: The model is the same, but the effect of each action is not. Reading and changing data carry different risk.

questions.prompt: Every row says "Approval: none". What change fits the sources best?

options.text: Keep no approvals, so the reps save time; review the logs at the end of each quarter.
options.explanation: A quarterly review finds a wrong email to a client months too late. The MCP spec says there should always be a human who can deny tool calls.

options.text: Require approval for every read and every write, and remove the CRM search entirely.
options.explanation: This blocks the useful, low-risk part. The lesson's rule is to match approval to the risk of the action.

options.text: Ask the model in the prompt to "be careful with deals and emails" instead of approvals.
options.explanation: An instruction is not a control. The docs describe approval as a setting in the system, not a request to the model.

options.text: Require a person to approve rows 2 and 3 before they run, and let the reads run directly.
options.explanation: Right. OpenAI's MCP guide lets the developer require explicit approval for tool calls, and the MCP spec says a human should be able to deny them.

questions.prompt: The plan builds a separate custom link for each AI app to each system. What does Anthropic's post on code execution with MCP suggest?

options.text: Custom links per pair are best, because each link can be tuned to one app.
options.explanation: The post describes one custom integration per pairing as the problem: it causes duplicated effort and is hard to scale.

options.text: Use a shared protocol such as MCP, so the work isn't repeated for every pair.
options.explanation: Right. The post says custom integrations for each pairing create duplicated effort, and that implementing MCP once unlocks an ecosystem of integrations.

options.text: Connect only one AI app to one system, because more links always mean less safety.
options.explanation: The post doesn't say to limit the number of connections. It says to stop building a custom one for every pair.

options.text: Skip integrations and paste data from each system into the chat by hand each day.
options.explanation: That doesn't scale for 90 reps and goes out of date fast. The post's answer is a shared protocol.
